lead: A helical gear has its teeth cut on a slant to the shaft axis. Contact begins at one end of a tooth and spreads across the face, so several teeth share the load and each engages gently: the drive is quieter and stronger than a spur pair of the same size. The same slant pushes the shaft along its axis, and that axial thrust changes the shaft and bearing design. Helical pairs are the default in vehicle gearboxes, electric-vehicle reducers and industrial speed reducers.
prereq: You need: the Lewis and Buckingham checks of spur gear design.

sections.h3: Helix angle and the two modules

blocks.text: The teeth lie at the helix angle ψ to the shaft axis; 15° to 25° is usual (some syllabi write β). Two planes matter. The normal plane is perpendicular to the tooth; the transverse plane is perpendicular to the shaft. The hob cuts the tooth in the normal plane, so the normal module mn and the normal pressure angle φn are the standard values. In the transverse plane:
mt = mn / cos ψ, d = mt z = mn z / cos ψ mt is the transverse module in mm and d the pitch diameter in mm. The pressure angles are related by tan φn = tan φt cos ψ. The axial pitch is pa = πmn/sin ψ.

Gears on parallel shafts must have opposite hands: one right-hand, one left-hand. The centre distance is a = m<sub>n</sub>(z<sub>1</sub> + z<sub>2</sub>)/(2 cos ψ), so a small change of ψ lets the designer hit a round centre distance without changing the module.

sections.h3: Virtual teeth and the strength checks

blocks.text: Cut a helical tooth by the normal plane. The plane meets the pitch cylinder in an ellipse whose radius of curvature at the tooth is r/cos²ψ, larger than the pitch radius r. In that plane the tooth looks like the tooth of a bigger spur gear with the virtual (formative) number of teeth zv = z/cos³ψ. The Lewis form factor is read for zv, and the tooth section is measured with mn:

Sb = σb b mn Y (Y for zv) Sb is the beam strength in N, b the face width in mm (often 10mn to 15mn). For the first sizing, helical teeth engage more gently than spur teeth, so the velocity factor is larger: Cv = 5.6/(5.6 + √v), and Feff = Cs Ft/Cv.
Buckingham's dynamic load and the wear strength take the helix angle into account:
Fd = 21v(Ceb cos²ψ + Ft) cos ψ / (21v + √(Ceb cos²ψ + Ft)) with the symbols of the spur gear check; then Feff = Cs Ft + Fd.
S<sub>w</sub> = b Q d<sub>1</sub> K / cos²ψ
blocks.where: with Q = 2z<sub>2</sub>/(z<sub>1</sub> + z<sub>2</sub>) and K = 0.16(BHN/100)² for a steel pair. Both checks need a factor of safety, S<sub>b</sub> ≥ f<sub>s</sub> F<sub>eff</sub> and S<sub>w</sub> ≥ f<sub>s</sub> F<sub>eff</sub>.

blocks.text: The overlap ratio b sin ψ/(πmn) counts how many axial pitches fit in the face width. Above 1, there is always a second tooth in contact along the face, which is where the quiet running comes from.
The tooth force has three components. With F<sub>t</sub> = P/v = 2T/d:
Fr = Ft tan φn / cos ψ, Fa = Ft tan ψ Fr is the radial (separating) force and Fa the axial thrust, both in N.

The thrust pushes the shaft along its axis, so one bearing on each shaft must be able to take it (an angular contact ball or taper roller bearing); the other is left free to float. Reversing the rotation, or the hand, reverses the thrust. A double helical (herringbone) gear has two opposite helices on one body: the two thrusts cancel inside the gear and the bearings see almost none, so ψ can be 30° to 45°; it costs more to make. Choosing ψ is a trade: a larger angle gives smoother contact and more overlap but more thrust. The bearing loads go to the selection of gearbox bearings and of rolling contact bearings.

examples.question: A helical pair has m<sub>n</sub> = 3 mm, z<sub>1</sub> = 20, z<sub>2</sub> = 80, ψ = 15°, φ<sub>n</sub> = 20° and b = 45 mm, and transmits 11 kW at 1450 rpm of the pinion. Find m<sub>t</sub>, d<sub>1</sub>, v, the three force components on the pinion, z<sub>v1</sub> and the overlap ratio.
steps: Transverse module: m<sub>t</sub> = 3/cos 15° = 3/0.96593 = 3.106 mm. Pitch diameters: d<sub>1</sub> = 3.106 × 20 = 62.12 mm, d<sub>2</sub> = 248.47 mm; a = 155.29 mm.
Pitch line velocity: v = π × 0.06212 × 1450/60 = 4.716 m/s.
examples.answer: m<sub>t</sub> = 3.106 mm, d<sub>1</sub> = 62.12 mm, v = 4.716 m/s, F<sub>t</sub> = 2332 N, F<sub>a</sub> = 625 N, F<sub>r</sub> = 879 N, z<sub>v1</sub> = 22.19, overlap ratio 1.24.

examples.question: Check the same pair for bending and wear. Both gears are steel with σ<sub>b</sub> = 200 N/mm² and 350 BHN; the drive is smooth (C<sub>s</sub> = 1.0); e = 0.010 mm, C = 11 400 N/mm²; required factor of safety 1.5.
steps: Weaker member: the pinion (z<sub>v2</sub> = 80/0.90122 = 88.8 gives a larger Y). Y<sub>1</sub> = 0.484 − 2.87/22.19 = 0.3547.
examples.answer: Factor of safety 1.58 in bending and 1.55 in wear: the pair is safe, and wear is slightly closer to its limit.

traps: Using m<sub>t</sub> in the beam strength. The Lewis section is the normal section, so use m<sub>n</sub>, and Y read for z<sub>v</sub> = z/cos³ψ, not z.
Writing F<sub>r</sub> = F<sub>t</sub> tan φ<sub>n</sub> without dividing by cos ψ, or using tan φ<sub>t</sub> and dividing again.
Forgetting the axial thrust F<sub>a</sub> = F<sub>t</sub> tan ψ in the shaft and bearing loads; in side view the gear looks like a spur gear, but the thrust is real.
Giving both gears of a parallel-shaft pair the same hand. They must be of opposite hand.
Using the spur velocity factor 3/(3 + v) for helical gears; helical teeth use 5.6/(5.6 + √v).

quiz.q: Define helix angle and normal module.
quiz.a: The helix angle ψ is the angle between a tooth and the shaft axis. The normal module m<sub>n</sub> is the module in the plane normal to the tooth; it is the standard cutter value.

quiz.q: Write the relation between the normal and transverse pressure angles.
quiz.a: tan φ<sub>n</sub> = tan φ<sub>t</sub> cos ψ.

quiz.q: Why is a helical pair quieter than a spur pair of the same size, and what new load appears?
quiz.a: Contact starts at one end of a tooth and spreads across the face, and with an overlap ratio above 1 another tooth is always engaged, so there is no sudden full-width impact. The new load is the axial thrust F<sub>t</sub> tan ψ.

quiz.q: A helical gear has m<sub>n</sub> = 4 mm, ψ = 20° and z = 25. Find m<sub>t</sub>, d and z<sub>v</sub>.
F<sub>t</sub> = 3000 N, ψ = 18°, φ<sub>n</sub> = 20°. Find F<sub>a</sub> and F<sub>r</sub>.
Why is the form factor read for z/cos³ψ and not for z?
quiz.a: In the normal plane the pitch cylinder appears as an ellipse with radius of curvature r/cos²ψ at the tooth, so the tooth has the shape of a tooth on a spur gear of diameter d/cos²ψ, which has z/cos³ψ teeth. That larger count gives a larger Y, which is the real tooth shape.

quiz.q: Why does a herringbone gear allow a larger helix angle?
quiz.a: Its two opposite helices produce equal and opposite thrusts that cancel inside the gear, so a large angle (30° to 45°) does not load the bearings axially.

beyond: Not for the exam. Helical gears are the default in electric-vehicle reducers and wind-turbine gearboxes, where whine matters as much as strength. Design software adds lead crowning and profile modification so contact stays away from the tooth ends under load. Researchers model mesh stiffness and transmission error to predict noise before a gear is cut. Search for helical gear transmission error, lead crowning and gear whine.
